scenes.heading: The four kinds of agent memory

cards.title: Conversation history
cards.body: The messages list. Exact, but it grows every turn.

cards.title: Short-term window
cards.body: Only the last few turns are sent. Cheap, but old details fall out.

cards.title: Summary memory
cards.body: Old turns compressed into a short summary. Keeps the gist.

cards.title: Long-term memory
cards.body: Facts saved in a database. Survives restarts and new chats.

scenes.title: Pause and try: predict the reply
scenes.body: The history is `[user: "I love chess", assistant: "Nice!"]`. Your code then sends **only** `[user: "What do I love?"]`.

items.text: What can the model answer? Why? What would you change?

items.q: Does the Claude API remember earlier messages?
items.a: No. The Messages API is **stateless**: each request stands alone. A conversation works because **your code** resends the history (user and assistant messages, in order) with every request.
items.trap: Saying "the model remembers our chat". Any memory is data your code stores and sends.

items.q: Why can't you just keep the whole history forever?
items.a: Cost and limits. Every turn resends everything, so input tokens and **latency** grow with the conversation, and eventually it won't fit the **context window**. You need a strategy: windows, summaries, long-term facts.
items.trap: Thinking that's only about money. Very long contexts also make replies slower.

options: The code doesn't append replies and messages to the history it sends
scenes.explain: The API is stateless. If a message isn't in the list you send, the model never sees it.

captions.text: Welcome to Module 6.
Your agents can now think in a loop and use tools safely.
But close the program, and they forget everything.
Even inside one chat, they only remember what you send them.
By the end of this module, you'll build a persistent study companion: it remembers
your name, your goals and what you find hard, across days, in a real database, with
privacy controls.
In this lesson, you'll learn what stateless means for a model API.
You'll prove it, by asking the same question with and without history.
You'll build a chat loop that keeps the conversation.
And you'll meet the four kinds of memory an agent can have.
Let's start with an everyday picture.
Imagine a brilliant tutor, with one strange problem.
The moment you leave the room, they forget you completely.
Your name, your last lesson, everything.
You can still get great help.
You just have to bring your notebook every time, and show them what you covered
before.
The tutor is the model.
Very smart, but it remembers nothing between visits.
The notebook is the list of messages you send with every request.
And carrying the notebook is your code's job, on every single call.
That's what stateless means.
Each request to the API stands alone.
The server doesn't keep your conversation between calls.
If the model seems to remember, it's because your code sent the history again.
Let's prove it with code.
The code is on the left, and what it printed is on the right.
As in every module, no API key is needed.
A scripted fake plays the model, and the first output line says so.
The important thing: like a real model, the fake only knows what is inside the
request.
This small function sends a list of messages, and returns the text of the reply.
Call one.
We say: hi, my name is Anuj.
Call two is a brand new request, with only the question: what's my name?
And the answer is: I don't know.
Nothing in this request says it.
Call one is gone.
Call three sends the earlier messages again: our introduction, the reply, and then
the question.
Now the answer is: your name is Anuj.
Same model, same question.
The only difference is what we sent.
Now, how does a normal chat work, then?
The first request has one message: the user's.
The API answers and forgets.
For the second request, your code sends three messages: the first user message, the
assistant's reply, and the new user message.
The third request sends five.
The conversation grows by two messages every turn, and the whole thing travels with
every request.
Keep this picture in mind: it's the reason for everything in the next two lessons.
Here's a real chat loop.
One list, history, holds the whole conversation.
Each line of input becomes a user message, appended to the list.
For a repeatable demo, the three lines come from a small text file.
Then we send the whole list, every time.
And we append the reply as an assistant message.
Forget this line, and the model never sees its own earlier answers.
Turn one: two messages stored, and thirteen input tokens sent.
Turn two: what's my name?
Anuj, because the history went with the request.
And look at the input tokens: thirteen, sixty-one, ninety.
Every turn sends more.
You pay for input tokens on every call, and the model has a maximum it can read.
That's the problem we solve in lessons two and three.
Let's name the kinds of memory an agent can have.
First, conversation history: the messages list.
Exact, but it grows every turn.
Second, a short-term window: send only the last few turns.
Cheap, but old details fall out.
Third, summary memory: old turns compressed into a short summary that keeps the
gist.
And fourth, long-term memory: facts saved in a database, which survive a restart,
and a brand new chat the next day.
Where does each one live?
History lives in a Python list, and it's lost when the program exits.
The window is just the part of the list you send.
A turn is lost from the request when it slides out.
The summary is a string, sent with the system prompt.
Details are lost if they don't make it into the summary.
And long-term memory lives in a database file.
It's only lost when you delete it, on purpose.
Pause the video and try this.
The history so far is: user says, I love chess.
Assistant says, nice.
Then your code sends a new request with only: what do I love?
What can the model answer, and why?
And what would you change in the code?
It can't know.
The request doesn't mention chess, and the API keeps nothing between calls.
The fix: append every message to the history list, and send the whole list each
time.
Interview corner.
Does the Claude API remember earlier messages?
A good answer: no.
The Messages API is stateless.
Each request stands alone.
A conversation works because your code resends the history, the user and assistant
messages in order, with every request.
The trap is saying the model remembers your chat.
Any memory is data your code stores, and sends.
A follow-up: why not just keep the whole history forever?
Because of cost and limits.
Every turn resends everything, so input tokens, and the time to answer, grow with
the conversation.
And eventually, it won't fit the context window.
So you need a strategy: windows, summaries, and long-term facts.
The trap is thinking it's only about money.
Long contexts also make every reply slower.
Quick check.
Your chatbot forgets what the user said two messages ago.
What's the most likely bug?
The code doesn't append every message to the history it sends.
The model only sees what's in the request.
Let's recap.
The API is stateless.
Each request stands alone.
A conversation is your code resending the history, every time.
Append the user's message, and the reply.
And the history grows every turn, which costs money and time, and hits limits.
Next lesson: short-term memory.
You'll measure how fast the conversation grows, meet the context window, and keep
only the turns that matter, without breaking tool calls.
